items.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
items.summary: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls. Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call. For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension. For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer. Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. (We’re also benchmarking ThunderPhone on more public benchmarks - stay tuned.) The downside is configuration complexity. Every agent benefits from a different setup on the ThunderPhone stack, and even individual call turns on the same call often benefit from different stacks. Configuring this manually worked for enterprise customers, but made it prohibitive to give smaller self-serve customers the full benefits without giving their agents our full attention. That’s how Zeus came about. Our enterprise configurations were repetitive enough that an AI could do them once we taught it how and gave it the right tools. We’re big fans of Claude Code and Codex for software development, but they fall short at configuring voice agents for a few reasons. First, unlike software development, where you can compile code and run tests to verify things work, you can’t run live calls inside a computer right after configuring a voice agent - and coding agents don’t know how to run simulated calls out of the box, or “listen” to a call to spot real problems. We built both capabilities into Zeus, giving it a “closed loop” experience building, testing, and improving voice agents just like coding agents have with regular software. Second, coding agents are pretty gullible about marketing claims. Companies building AI and voice infrastructure commonly post the most favorable possible interpretation of their capabilities online. Claude and Codex read those claims, believe them uncritically, and pick tools based on marketing rather than real performance. At best, that leads to suboptimal architectural choices; at worst, to voice agents that don’t really work at all. We’ve sidestepped this with continuous evals feeding an internal knowledge base. For everything that matters for voice agents - accurate audio understanding, instruction following, noise cancelling, turn-taking, and more - we maintain internal benchmarks built on real call data. Every time a new AI model comes out, we (now mostly automatically) feed it through our evals for performance, speed, cost, and reliability/consistency. That feeds our internal knowledge base, which Zeus uses to pick the right stack for every agent, call, and conversation turn. This all happens behind the scenes to keep the ThunderPhone experience seamless. A user just describes their use case and goals, and Zeus helps fill in ambiguities, connect VoIP and software integrations, and optimize the voice agent(s) on simulated and live calls until they hit the highest performance on business goals (conversions, unit economics, etc.) possible with today’s models. Zeus is also differentiated on cost. Zeus itself is free to use for now, though we expect to move to subscription or token-based pricing later. For calls, we’ve become the first voice AI vendor to our knowledge to charge on a cost-plus basis: ThunderPhone customers pay exactly what we pay our vendors, plus a 17% margin on calls costing 2c/min or less, scaling linearly up to 25% for calls costing us 15c/min or more, and 25% from there on up. However, we find that simple phone agents do well on a stack that costs about 2c/min, and more complex cases typically land around 5-10c/min - significantly cheaper than most alternatives. Zeus is brand-new, so we’re eager to get feedback on how it works for customers, and any areas we could improve it. Give it a try and see what you think - let me know if you have any feedback or questions. Alex

items.title: Gke-sandboxes: Agent sandboxes with filesystem snapshots at 1.9¢/hour
items.story_key: story|ver:1.9|title:gke sandboxes agent sandboxes with filesystem snapshots at 1 9 hour
items.content_excerpt: Give each cloud agent its own Linux sandbox, in your own Google Cloud project. A sandbox runs commands and keeps files. Put it to sleep while the user is away, and open the same ID later to get the files back. A 2 vCPU / 4 GB sandbox costs about 1.9¢ for each hour it is awake , cluster overhead included. Daytona and E2B list 16.6¢ for the same hour. A sleeping sandbox costs only its storage. The agent deploys the cluster with Terraform, runs the verifier, and shows you how to connect your backend. Or deploy it by hand . Costs are for one sandbox at 2 vCPU and 4 GB. Managed providers are at list prices for compute and storage only. Timings used 4 vCPU and 8 GB. Every bar in the chart above prices the same mostly idle sandbox, at the 0.076 vCPU that Energy’s running sandboxes averaged, about 4% of 2 vCPU. Daytona, E2B and Fly.io charge for the full size while it runs. Vercel charges for the CPU in use and all of the memory. Modal charges for what is used. The GKE figure is a whole cluster bill divided by its sandboxes: 520 awake at 56 to a machine, with two spare machines, node disks, system nodes, the cluster fee and snapshot storage. It needs that scale. A small cluster still pays for its minimum machines. Over a 730-hour month awake, 1.9¢ an hour is $14.22. Packed tighter on C4D machines, the GKE compute estimate falls to about $7.80 a month, or 1.1¢ an hour. A sleeping sandbox is a snapshot in Cloud Storage. Machines you keep running still appear on your bill. Medians. The GKE start time is with two sandboxes kept ready; without one it is about 2.7 s. The other providers were timed by Sandbox Bench from a different region, so read the rows as neighbors, not a ranking. GKE wakes slower than most, and slower still with many files: about 6.5 s at 25,000 files. Building Better Auth took 67 s on a C4D machine with one sandbox, and 81 s on a machine packed with 95 idle ones. We have no build timings for the managed providers. gke-sandboxes restores files, not running processes. E2B can keep memory through sleep. The trade is that you run the cluster: capacity, upgrades and recovery are yours. A managed provider is the better choice if you need only a handful of sandboxes, running processes that survive sleep, GPUs, or a VM kernel per sandbox.

items.title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
items.story_key: story|ver:27|title:daisyrose 27b pushing the frontier of post training efficiency
items.content_excerpt: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. >50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app

items.story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
items.content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective. items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.content_excerpt: Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.summary:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

items.content_excerpt: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments that frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta use to train and evaluate their models. Labs improve agent capability by giving them difficult tasks that Abundant designs, letting the model attempt it, and grading the result as pass or fail. Each task is an RL rollout with a full environment. The model needs instructions, a defined goal, and a verifier to decide whether the task was completed. But it also needs infrastructure: compute to power the run, Dockerfiles, and isolation. Depending on the task, an agent may even need accelerators like GPUs. Abundant has created over 75,000 rollouts — ranging from GPU kernel optimization to long-horizon coding — each of which runs in a Modal Sandbox. Modal makes their rollout infrastructure easy to build and cost-efficient to run, enabling the Abundant team to focus on their core business. Today, almost all of Abundant’s rollout platform runs on Modal. Modal Functions power Abundant’s scheduler API to start tasks, clean up dead runs, and review rollouts. Modal Sandboxes power the rollout environments. Abundant initially chose to evaluate Sandbox providers because they wanted to avoid managing EC2 clusters directly, which would pull engineering time away from their core business of building RL environments. Modal enabled them to build their infrastructure directly in code, launch Sandboxes easily via API, and elastically scale their traffic as business grew. As of November 2026, Abundant runs over two million Sandboxes per month. Modal worked with the Abundant team to design and build their rollout architecture, focusing on designing a system that didn’t leave Abundant having to pay heavily for idle compute. Each rollout has a few steps: launch the task, attempt the task, verify the work, and report the work. Throughout the rollout, a “monitor” needs to verify that the Sandbox is still active. While Abundant had considered hosting the monitor outside of the Sandbox, they ultimately chose to include the rollout monitor inside the Sandbox and then used short-lived Modal Functions to start Sandboxes. The small rollout monitor inside the Sandbox makes periodic HTTP calls: a heartbeat every 30 seconds, live events, and the final result. If a Sandbox goes quiet, the control plane will attempt to connect three times before terminating it. items.title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
items.summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
items.story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
items.content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. items.title: Paul Stack: I'll Never Write Infrastructure as Code Again
items.summary:
Paul Stack helped build Terraform. Now he says he'll never write another line of infrastructure as code, because an agent harness runs his team's production infrastructure instead.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/kpo

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Guy Podjarny sits down with Paul, who spent years on Terraform at HashiCorp and on Pulumi before Swamp, to unpack why agents still trip over infrastructure state, what it takes to run a software factory that automates software delivery all the way to production, and why the people who know the system still make the calls. Then stay for Paul's full DevCon talk, From Page to Dossier, on a lights-out factory that does the 3am on-call legwork before anyone is woken up.

items.content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request.
